title: How Ebola Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Ebola: its 1976 discovery near the Ebola River in Zaire (now DR Congo) and the Sudan outbreak, the five species named for origin regions (including Reston, named for Reston, Virginia, where monkeys were shipped), the virus's RNA structure and how it hijacks cells, its attack on the immune system and resulting hemorrhagic fever and organ failure, symptoms and stages, the suspected fruit bat reservoir, transmission via bodily fluids, burial customs and needle exposure, prevention advice, the 2014 West Africa outbreak starting in Guinea, distrust of governments and health authorities, and the experimental ZMapp monoclonal antibody treatment given to American missionaries. The episode closes with a listener mail ad from Corey Barker and a note on Marburg virus.

segments.title: Opening banter and Atlanta patients
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by joking about the recording booth and a visit to the CDC museum, then discuss the two Ebola patients being treated at Emory in Atlanta after being flown from Liberia, the controversy over the move, and the movies Contagion and Outbreak.

segments.title: Discovery of Ebola in 1976
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1976 discovery, named for the Ebola River in what was then Zaire. They recount the index case Mabalo, whose needle was reused, and the outbreaks in Zaire and Sudan with their death tolls. They compare the mortality rate to the Spanish flu and note airborne spread among monkeys.

segments.title: Burial customs and the five Ebola species
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how burial rituals involving close contact with bodies spread the virus, then cover the filovirus family and the five Ebola species named for their regions, including Reston, Virginia, where infected crab-eating monkeys from the Philippines did not cause human illness.

segments.title: How Ebola infects cells
segments.summary: Explanation of Ebola's RNA genome, its small size compared with human DNA, and how it enters cells, hijacks them to replicate, and exits enveloped in lipid membranes. Ebola then targets immune cells, endothelial cells, and organs such as the liver and spleen. It also produces glycoproteins that suppress the immune response.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief break in the episode.

segments.title: Symptoms, stages, and bleeding
segments.summary: The hosts describe the incubation period, early flu-like symptoms often mistaken for malaria, later stages including bloody diarrhea, rash, and internal bleeding, and death from multi-organ failure and hypotensive shock. They note that victims do not typically bleed from the eyes as depicted in movies.

segments.title: Fruit bat reservoir and transmission
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the search for the natural reservoir, with fruit bats as the leading suspect, and how the virus has been transmitted through bat guano in the movie Contagion. They also cover transmission through bodily fluids and needles, and the differing fatality rates by exposure route and incubation periods.

segments.title: Prevention and the 2014 West Africa outbreak
segments.summary: Advice for avoiding infection, including avoiding bush meat, caves, forests, and reused needles. The hosts describe the spread from Guinea, the possible role of climate change in bat migration, and the distrust of governments and health authorities, including political blaming in Sierra Leone. They also describe the Guinea index case and village spread, and a health-monitoring bot that detected the outbreak early.

segments.title: ZMapp experimental treatment
segments.summary: The hosts report on the experimental drug ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody therapy made in tobacco plants, given to American missionaries Kent Brantly and Nancy Writebol, who recovered, while Miguel Pajares died. They discuss the WHO ethics panel and the ethics of using an unapproved drug, and note the 42-day rule for declaring an outbreak over.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener mail from Corey Barker about starting an audiobook career and offering a show ad, followed by the hosts' sign-off and website information. The hosts also briefly mention Marburg virus as a related deadly cousin.
